Introduction to CSS

Beginner ⏱️ 5 min read Updated: July 2026

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of a document written in HTML or XML. It defines how elements should be rendered on screen, on paper, in speech, or on other media.

Understanding Cascading

The term "Cascading" refers to the specific algorithm used by the browser to determine which style rules apply to an element when multiple rules conflict. It follows a hierarchy of priority, typically falling back from Inline styles > Internal/External stylesheets > Browser defaults.

Key Features of CSS

  • Separation of Concerns: Separates structure (HTML) from presentation (CSS).
  • Responsive Design: Allows creating websites that adapt to different screen sizes.
  • Reusability: One CSS file can style multiple HTML pages.
  • Maintainability: Easy to update the entire look of a website from a single file.

Advantages of CSS

Advantage Description
Faster Page Speed Less code means faster download times. Browsers cache external CSS files.
Superior Styles CSS offers far more styling capabilities than traditional HTML attributes.
Multiple Device Compatibility Styles can be customized for different devices (mobile, print, desktop).

CSS Syntax

A CSS rule-set consists of a selector and a declaration block:

CSS Syntax Structure
selector {
  property: value;
  another-property: another-value;
}

Example:

h1 {
  color: #10b981;
  font-size: 24px;
}

Here, h1 is the selector, color is the property, and #10b981 is the value.

Styling HTML: Inline, Internal & External CSS

Beginner ⏱️ 6 min read Updated: July 2026

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is used to style and format the layout of Web pages. There are three ways to insert CSS into an HTML document:

📌 Key Takeaways

  • Inline CSS: Applied directly inside an HTML element using the style attribute. Used for quick single-element overrides.
  • Internal CSS: Written inside a <style> block within the <head> section of the HTML file. Ideal for single-page documents.
  • External CSS: Defined in a separate .css file and linked using <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. Best practice for maintainable websites.

1. Inline CSS Example

Syntax: Inline Style Attribute
<h1 style="color: #10b981; font-size: 24px; text-align: center;">Hello World</h1>

2. Internal CSS Example

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <style>
    body {
      background-color: #0f172a;
      color: #f8fafc;
    }
    .heading {
      color: #38bdf8;
      font-weight: bold;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1 class="heading">Internal CSS Styling</h1>
</body>
</html>

3. External CSS Example

Link the external sheet inside HTML <head>:

<!-- index.html -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="css/main.css">

And write pure CSS rules inside main.css:

/* css/main.css */
.card {
  background: #1e293b;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 1px solid #334155;
}

CSS Box Model: Margin, Padding, Border & Content

Core Concept ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

All HTML elements can be considered as boxes. In CSS, the term Box Model is used when talking about design and layout. It wraps around every HTML element and consists of four layers.

📦 Box Model Architecture

  • Content: The real content of the element, where text and images appear.
  • Padding: Clears an area around the content. Padding is inside the border and is transparent.
  • Border: A border that goes around the padding and content.
  • Margin: Clears an area outside the border. Margin is completely transparent and separates elements.
Box Model Breakdown Diagram
MARGIN (Outer spacing)
BORDER (Element boundary)
PADDING (Inner spacing)
CONTENT (Text / Images / Elements)

CSS Box Sizing: content-box vs border-box

/* Standard CSS Reset rule */
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box; /* Includes padding and border in total width/height */
}

.box {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid #10b981;
  margin: 15px;
}

💡 Pro Tip

Always set box-sizing: border-box globally. Without it, adding padding or borders increases the actual element width beyond your specified width property!

CSS Selectors & Specificity Hierarchy

Essential ⏱️ 10 min read Updated: July 2026

CSS Selectors target HTML elements to apply styles. When multiple conflicting rules apply to an element, CSS uses Specificity rules to decide which style wins.

Types of CSS Selectors

Selector Type Syntax Example Description
Universal * Selects all HTML elements on the page.
Element / Tag p, h1, div Selects all elements with the specified tag name.
Class Selector .btn, .card Selects elements with the specified class attribute.
ID Selector #header, #main Selects a single unique element with the specified ID.
Attribute Selector [type="text"] Selects elements based on an attribute or attribute value.
Pseudo-Class :hover, :nth-child(2) Selects elements based on state or DOM position.
Pseudo-Element ::before, ::after Styles specific parts of an element or injects content.

CSS Specificity Hierarchy Score

📊 Specificity Calculation (Inline > ID > Class > Tag)

  1. Inline Style: (1, 0, 0, 0) - Highest weight (e.g. style="...")
  2. ID Selectors: (0, 1, 0, 0) - (e.g. #navbar)
  3. Classes, Attributes, Pseudo-classes: (0, 0, 1, 0) - (e.g. .btn:hover)
  4. Elements & Pseudo-elements: (0, 0, 0, 1) - (e.g. h1::first-letter)

Note: !important overrides all normal specificity rules. Use sparingly!

/* Specificity Example */
p { color: white; }                  /* (0,0,0,1) */
.text-green { color: #10b981; }      /* (0,0,1,0) - Wins over tag */
#main-text { color: #38bdf8; }       /* (0,1,0,0) - Wins over class */

/* Attribute & Pseudo-class */
input[type="submit"]:hover {
  background-color: #059669;
}

CSS Combinators: Relationships Between Elements

Intermediate ⏱️ 7 min read Updated: July 2026

A combinator explains the relationship between selectors. CSS includes four different combinator types to target nested or sibling elements precisely.

The 4 CSS Combinators

Combinator Name Symbol Rule Example Matching Description
Descendant Combinator (space) div p Matches all <p> elements inside a <div>, regardless of nesting depth.
Child Combinator > div > p Matches only direct children <p> elements immediately inside <div>.
Adjacent Sibling + h2 + p Matches the single <p> element directly after an <h2>.
General Sibling ~ h2 ~ p Matches all <p> elements that are siblings following an <h2>.

Combinator Code Example

/* 1. Descendant */
.container span {
  color: #fbbf24; /* Targets all spans inside .container */
}

/* 2. Direct Child */
.menu > li {
  display: inline-block; /* Targets only top-level li items */
}

/* 3. Adjacent Sibling */
h2 + p {
  font-size: 1.1rem;
  font-weight: 600; /* First paragraph after H2 */
}

/* 4. General Sibling */
.active ~ .item {
  opacity: 0.7; /* All subsequent sibling .item elements */
}

Styling Images: Responsive Layouts & Object Fit

Practical ⏱️ 6 min read Updated: July 2026

Images play a crucial role in modern responsive UI design. Key properties include object-fit, aspect-ratio, borders, shadows, and hover scale effects.

Key Image Properties

  • max-width: 100%: Prevents images from overflowing parent containers.
  • object-fit: cover: Crops and scales images cleanly to fit containers without distortion.
  • aspect-ratio: 16 / 9: Preserves explicit proportions across screens.
  • filter: Applies visual adjustments like grayscale(), blur(), or drop-shadow().
/* Responsive Card Image */
.card-img {
  width: 100%;
  height: 220px;
  object-fit: cover;
  border-radius: 8px;
  box-shadow: 0 10px 25px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.4);
  transition: transform 0.4s ease, filter 0.4s ease;
}

.card-img:hover {
  transform: scale(1.03);
  filter: brightness(1.1);
}

Styling HTML5 Audio & Video Elements

Media UI ⏱️ 5 min read Updated: July 2026

HTML5 <audio> and <video> elements can be styled with custom borders, responsive fluid wrappers, aspect ratio boxes, and controls overlays.

Responsive Video Wrapper Pattern

/* Fluid 16:9 Video Container */
.video-container {
  position: relative;
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  border-radius: 12px;
  overflow: hidden;
  border: 1px solid #334155;
  box-shadow: 0 20px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6);
}

.video-container video {
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
}

/* Audio Player Custom Styling */
audio {
  width: 100%;
  accent-color: #10b981; /* Styles native browser media controls */
  border-radius: 30px;
}

Styling HTML Tables: Borders, Zebra Striping & Responsiveness

Data UI ⏱️ 7 min read Updated: July 2026

Default HTML tables look plain. CSS transforms tables into clean, readable data grids using border-collapse, cell padding, zebra-striping, hover states, and responsive scroll wrappers.

.custom-table {
  width: 100%;
  border-collapse: collapse;
  margin-top: 1rem;
  font-size: 0.95rem;
}

.custom-table th {
  background-color: #1e293b;
  color: #10b981;
  padding: 12px 16px;
  text-align: left;
  border-bottom: 2px solid #334155;
}

.custom-table td {
  padding: 12px 16px;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #334155;
}

/* Zebra Striping */
.custom-table tbody tr:nth-child(even) {
  background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.02);
}

/* Row Hover Effect */
.custom-table tbody tr:hover {
  background-color: rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.1);
}

Styling Forms: Inputs, Focus States & Custom Buttons

Interactive UI ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

Form controls require careful CSS styling for optimal user experience (UX) and accessibility. Focus rings, placeholder text, validation highlights, and submit buttons should respond to user action smoothly.

/* Form Input Styling */
.form-input {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 12px 16px;
  background: #0f172a;
  border: 1px solid #334155;
  border-radius: 6px;
  color: #f8fafc;
  font-size: 1rem;
  transition: border-color 0.3s, box-shadow 0.3s;
}

/* Accessible Focus Outline */
.form-input:focus {
  outline: none;
  border-color: #10b981;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.25);
}

/* Form Button */
.btn-submit {
  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #10b981, #059669);
  color: white;
  padding: 12px 24px;
  border: none;
  border-radius: 6px;
  font-weight: 600;
  cursor: pointer;
  transition: transform 0.2s, box-shadow 0.2s;
}

.btn-submit:hover {
  transform: translateY(-2px);
  box-shadow: 0 8px 20px rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.4);
}

CSS Positioning: Static, Relative, Absolute, Fixed & Sticky

Layout Engine ⏱️ 9 min read Updated: July 2026

The position property specifies the type of positioning method used for an element (static, relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky).

Position Value Behavior Description Offset Properties Supported
static Default position. Elements render in normal document flow. No (top, left, etc. ignored)
relative Positioned relative to its normal position without removing it from flow. Yes (top, right, bottom, left)
absolute Removed from flow. Positioned relative to nearest positioned ancestor (non-static). Yes (top, right, bottom, left)
fixed Removed from flow. Positioned relative to viewport; stays in place during scroll. Yes (top, right, bottom, left)
sticky Toggles between relative and fixed depending on scroll position. Yes (e.g. top: 0)

Positioning Code Example

/* Parent relative container */
.card-container {
  position: relative;
  width: 300px;
  height: 200px;
  background: #1e293b;
}

/* Absolute Badge positioned at top right */
.badge-top {
  position: absolute;
  top: 10px;
  right: 10px;
  background: #ef4444;
  color: white;
  padding: 4px 10px;
  border-radius: 20px;
  font-size: 0.75rem;
}

/* Sticky Header */
.sticky-nav {
  position: sticky;
  top: 0;
  z-index: 1000;
  background: #0f172a;
}

CSS Display Property: Block, Inline, Inline-Block & None

Foundations ⏱️ 6 min read Updated: July 2026

The display property is the most important CSS property for controlling layout. It determines how an element renders in the document tree.

🔍 Display Values Overview

  • block: Starts on a new line and takes up full width (e.g., <div>, <p>, <h1>). Accepts width, height, margins, and paddings.
  • inline: Does not start on a new line, takes only required width (e.g., <span>, <a>). Does NOT respect top/bottom width, height, or vertical margins!
  • inline-block: Formatted like an inline element, but accepts width, height, padding, and margin properties.
  • none: Hides element completely; removes it from document layout flow.
.nav-item {
  display: inline-block; /* Inline horizontal flow with custom width/padding */
  width: 120px;
  padding: 10px;
  text-align: center;
}

.hidden-element {
  display: none; /* Completely invisible & occupies no space */
}

topics.content:

CSS Flexbox: 1D Flexible Box Layout Model

Modern Layout ⏱️ 20 min read Updated: July 2026

Introduction to Flexbox: The Flexible Box Layout Module, commonly referred to as Flexbox, was designed as a one-dimensional layout model. It offers space distribution between items in an interface and powerful alignment capabilities. Flexbox provides a more efficient way to lay out, align, and distribute space among items in a container, even when their size is unknown and/or dynamic (thus the word "flex").

A flex layout allows the container to alter its items' width/height (and order) to best fill the available space (mostly to accommodate to all kind of display devices and screen sizes). A flex container expands items to fill available free space or shrinks them to prevent overflow. Most importantly, the flexbox layout is direction-agnostic as opposed to the regular layouts (block which is vertically-based and inline which is horizontally-based). While those work well for pages, they lack flexibility (no pun intended) to support large or complex applications, especially when it comes to orientation changing, resizing, stretching, shrinking, etc.

Flex Container Properties (Parent)

  • display: flex | inline-flex;: This defines a flex container; inline or block depending on the given value. It enables a flex context for all its direct children. Note that CSS columns have no effect on a flex container.
  • flex-direction: row | row-reverse | column | column-reverse;: This establishes the main-axis, thus defining the direction flex items are placed in the flex container. Flexbox is (usually) a single-direction layout concept. Think of flex items as primarily laying out either in horizontal rows or vertical columns.
    • row (default): left to right in ltr; right to left in rtl.
    • row-reverse: right to left in ltr; left to right in rtl.
    • column: same as row but top to bottom.
    • column-reverse: same as row-reverse but bottom to top.
  • flex-wrap: nowrap | wrap | wrap-reverse;: By default, flex items will all try to fit onto one line. You can change that and allow the items to wrap as needed with this property.
    • nowrap (default): all flex items will be on one line.
    • wrap: flex items will wrap onto multiple lines, from top to bottom.
    • wrap-reverse: flex items will wrap onto multiple lines from bottom to top.
  • flex-flow: This is a shorthand for the flex-direction and flex-wrap properties, which together define the flex container's main and cross axes. The default value is row nowrap.
  • justify-content: flex-start | flex-end | center | space-between | space-around | space-evenly;: This defines the alignment along the main axis. It helps distribute extra free space leftover when either all the flex items on a line are inflexible, or are flexible but have reached their maximum size. It also exerts some control over the alignment of items when they overflow the line.
    • flex-start (default): items are packed toward the start of the flex-direction.
    • flex-end: items are packed toward the end of the flex-direction.
    • center: items are centered along the line.
    • space-between: items are evenly distributed in the line; first item is on the start line, last item on the end line.
    • space-around: items are evenly distributed in the line with equal space around them. Note that visually the spaces aren't equal, since all the items have equal space on both sides. The first item will have one unit of space against the container edge, but two units of space between the next item because that next item has its own spacing that applies.
    • space-evenly: items are distributed so that the spacing between any two items (and the space to the edges) is equal.
  • align-items: stretch | flex-start | flex-end | center | baseline;: This defines the default behavior for how flex items are laid out along the cross axis on the current line. Think of it as the justify-content version for the cross-axis (perpendicular to the main-axis).
    • stretch (default): stretch to fill the container (still respect min-width/max-width).
    • flex-start / start / self-start: items are placed at the start of the cross axis.
    • flex-end / end / self-end: items are placed at the end of the cross axis.
    • center: items are centered in the cross-axis.
    • baseline: items are aligned such as their baselines align.
  • align-content: flex-start | flex-end | center | space-between | space-around | space-evenly | stretch;: This aligns a flex container's lines within when there is extra space in the cross-axis, similar to how justify-content aligns individual items within the main-axis. Note: this property has no effect when there is only one line of flex items.

Flex Item Properties (Children)

  • order: <integer>;: By default, flex items are laid out in the source order. However, the order property controls the order in which they appear in the flex container. Negative values are allowed.
  • flex-grow: <number>;: This defines the ability for a flex item to grow if necessary. It accepts a unitless value that serves as a proportion. It dictates what amount of the available space inside the flex container the item should take up. If all items have flex-grow set to 1, the remaining space in the container will be distributed equally to all children. If one of the children has a value of 2, the remaining space would take up twice as much space as the others (or it will try to, at least). Default is 0.
  • flex-shrink: <number>;: This defines the ability for a flex item to shrink if necessary. Default is 1. Negative numbers are invalid.
  • flex-basis: <length> | auto;: This defines the default size of an element before the remaining space is distributed. It can be a length (e.g. 20%, 5rem, etc.) or a keyword. The auto keyword means "look at my width or height property".
  • flex: none | [ <'flex-grow'> <'flex-shrink'>? || <'flex-basis'> ];: This is the shorthand for flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis combined. The second and third parameters (flex-shrink and flex-basis) are optional. The default is 0 1 auto, but if you set it with a single number value, like flex: 5;, that changes the flex-basis to 0%, so it's like setting flex-grow: 5; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%;. It is recommended that you use this shorthand property rather than set the individual properties. The shorthand sets the other values intelligently.
  • align-self: auto | flex-start | flex-end | center | baseline | stretch;: This allows the default alignment (or the one specified by align-items) to be overridden for individual flex items. Note that float, clear and vertical-align have no effect on a flex item.

Common Flexbox Patterns & Best Practices

  • Perfect Centering: Before Flexbox, centering an element both horizontally and vertically was notoriously difficult. With Flexbox, it is incredibly simple. Just apply display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; to the parent container. The child element will be perfectly centered regardless of its dimensions or the dimensions of the container.
  • Holy Grail Layout: The Holy Grail layout consists of a header, a footer, and a main content area with two sidebars (left and right). Flexbox makes achieving this layout much easier than older float-based methods. Using flex-direction: column for the overall page structure and flex-direction: row for the main content area allows for flexible sidebars and a main content area that expands to fill the remaining space.
  • Sticky Footer: A common requirement is to have a footer that sticks to the bottom of the page when there is little content, but is pushed down by the content when there is a lot of it. Setting the body to display: flex; flex-direction: column; min-height: 100vh; and the main content area to flex: 1 ensures the main content grows to push the footer to the bottom.
  • Equal Height Columns: Flexbox naturally solves the equal height column problem. By default, flex items in a row will stretch to match the height of the tallest item in that row, provided align-items is set to stretch (which is the default).
  • Responsive Navigation Menus: Flexbox is perfect for creating responsive navigation menus. You can easily distribute space between menu items using justify-content: space-between or space-around, and allow items to wrap on smaller screens using flex-wrap: wrap.
  • Media Objects: The media object pattern (an image or icon on one side, with descriptive text alongside it) is a classic use case for Flexbox. The image can have a fixed size, while the text container uses flex-grow: 1 to fill the remaining space.
  • Form Layouts: Flexbox simplifies form layouts, such as aligning labels and inputs, or creating inline forms where elements sit side-by-side on large screens and stack on small screens.

Limitations of Flexbox

Flexbox is fundamentally a one-dimensional layout system. While you can create multi-line flex layouts using flex-wrap: wrap, the items on each line act independently of the items on other lines. You cannot easily align an item on the second row with an item on the first row to create a strict grid structure. This is where CSS Grid comes in. Performance can sometimes be an issue with very large, deeply nested flexbox structures, although modern browsers are highly optimized.

Key Flexbox Container Properties
.flex-container {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: row;        /* row | column | row-reverse | column-reverse */
  justify-content: space-between; /* flex-start | flex-end | center | space-between | space-around */
  align-items: center;        /* flex-start | flex-end | center | baseline | stretch */
  flex-wrap: wrap;            /* nowrap | wrap | wrap-reverse */
  gap: 1.5rem;                /* Gap spacing between flex items */
}

topics.title: CSS Grid Layout
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > CSS > Display & Layout

CSS Grid: 2D Grid-Based Layout System

Modern Layout ⏱️ 25 min read Updated: July 2026

Introduction to CSS Grid Layout: CSS Grid Layout (aka "Grid" or "CSS Grid"), is a two-dimensional grid-based layout system that, compared to any web layout system of the past, completely changes the way we design user interfaces. CSS has always been used to lay out our web pages, but it's never done a very good job of it. First, we used tables, then floats, positioning and inline-block, but all of these methods were essentially hacks and left out a lot of important functionality (vertical centering, for instance).

Flexbox helped out, but it's intended for simpler one-dimensional layouts, not complex two-dimensional ones (Flexbox and Grid actually work very well together). Grid is the first CSS module created specifically to solve the layout problems we've all been hacking our way around for as long as we've been making websites.

Grid Terminology

  • Grid Container: The element on which display: grid is applied. It's the direct parent of all the grid items.
  • Grid Item: The children (i.e. direct descendants) of the grid container.
  • Grid Line: The dividing lines that make up the structure of the grid. They can be either vertical ("column grid lines") or horizontal ("row grid lines") and reside on either side of a row or column.
  • Grid Track: The space between two adjacent grid lines. You can think of them like the columns or rows of the grid.
  • Grid Cell: The space between two adjacent row and two adjacent column grid lines. It's a single "unit" of the grid.
  • Grid Area: The total space surrounded by four grid lines. A grid area may be comprised of any number of grid cells.

Grid Container Properties (Parent)

  • display: grid | inline-grid;: Defines the element as a grid container and establishes a new grid formatting context for its contents.
  • grid-template-columns: <track-size> ... | <line-name> <track-size> ...; and grid-template-rows: <track-size> ... | <line-name> <track-size> ...;: These properties define the columns and rows of the grid with a space-separated list of values. The values represent the track size, and the space between them represents the grid line.
    • You can use standard length values (px, em, rem, %, vh, vw, etc.).
    • The fr unit: Grid introduces the fr unit, which represents a fraction of the available space in the grid container. For example, grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr; will create three columns where the middle one is twice as wide as the other two.
    • repeat() function: Allows you to repeat a pattern of tracks. For example, grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); is equivalent to grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;.
    • minmax() function: Defines a size range. For example, minmax(100px, 1fr) means the track will be at least 100px wide, but can grow to fill 1fr of the available space.
    • auto-fill and auto-fit: Used with repeat() to create dynamic, responsive grids without media queries. grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); will create as many 200px columns as will fit in the container, and then distribute the remaining space equally among them. auto-fit works similarly but collapses empty tracks.
  • grid-template-areas: "<grid-area-name> | . | none | ..." "...";: This property allows you to define a grid layout by referencing the names of the grid areas which are specified with the grid-area property on grid items. Repeating the name of a grid area causes the content to span those cells. A period signifies an empty cell. The syntax itself provides a visualization of the structure of the grid.
  • grid-template: A shorthand for setting grid-template-rows, grid-template-columns, and grid-template-areas in a single declaration.
  • column-gap: <line-size>; and row-gap: <line-size>;: Specifies the size of the grid lines. You can think of it like setting the width of the gutters between the columns/rows. gap is the shorthand for both.
  • justify-items: start | end | center | stretch;: Aligns grid items along the inline (row) axis (as opposed to align-items which aligns along the block (column) axis). This value applies to all grid items inside the container.
  • align-items: start | end | center | stretch;: Aligns grid items along the block (column) axis (as opposed to justify-items which aligns along the inline (row) axis). This value applies to all grid items inside the container.
  • place-items: <align-items> / <justify-items>;: place-items sets both the align-items and justify-items properties in a single declaration.
  • justify-content: start | end | center | stretch | space-around | space-between | space-evenly;: Sometimes the total size of your grid might be less than the size of its grid container. This property sets the alignment of the grid within the grid container along the inline (row) axis.
  • align-content: start | end | center | stretch | space-around | space-between | space-evenly;: This property sets the alignment of the grid within the grid container along the block (column) axis.
  • place-content: <align-content> / <justify-content>;: place-content sets both the align-content and justify-content properties in a single declaration.
  • grid-auto-columns: <track-size> ...; and grid-auto-rows: <track-size> ...;: Specifies the size of any auto-generated grid tracks (aka implicit grid tracks). Implicit tracks get created when there are more grid items than cells in the grid or when a grid item is placed outside of the explicit grid.
  • grid-auto-flow: row | column | row dense | column dense;: If you have grid items that you don't explicitly place on the grid, the auto-placement algorithm kicks in to automatically place the items. This property controls how the auto-placement algorithm works. dense attempts to fill in holes earlier in the grid if smaller items come up later, which may cause items to appear out of order.

Grid Item Properties (Children)

  • grid-column-start: <number> | <name> | span <number> | span <name> | auto;
  • grid-column-end: <number> | <name> | span <number> | span <name> | auto;
  • grid-row-start: <number> | <name> | span <number> | span <name> | auto;
  • grid-row-end: <number> | <name> | span <number> | span <name> | auto;
    • Determines a grid item's location within the grid by referring to specific grid lines. grid-column-start/grid-row-start is the line where the item begins, and grid-column-end/grid-row-end is the line where the item ends.
    • span <number> means the item will span across the provided number of grid tracks.
  • grid-column: <start-line> / <end-line> | <start-line> / span <value>; and grid-row: <start-line> / <end-line> | <start-line> / span <value>;: Shorthand for grid-column-start + grid-column-end, and grid-row-start + grid-row-end, respectively.
  • grid-area: <name> | <row-start> / <column-start> / <row-end> / <column-end>;: Gives an item a name so that it can be referenced by a template created with the grid-template-areas property. Alternatively, this property can be used as an even shorter shorthand for grid-row-start + grid-column-start + grid-row-end + grid-column-end.
  • justify-self: start | end | center | stretch;: Aligns a grid item inside a cell along the inline (row) axis (as opposed to align-self which aligns along the block (column) axis). This value applies to the content inside a single grid item.
  • align-self: start | end | center | stretch;: Aligns a grid item inside a cell along the block (column) axis (as opposed to justify-self which aligns along the inline (row) axis). This value applies to the content inside a single grid item.
  • place-self: <align-self> / <justify-self>;: place-self sets both the align-self and justify-self properties in a single declaration.

Advanced Grid Techniques & Patterns

  • RAM (Repeat, Auto, Minmax): This is one of the most powerful techniques in CSS Grid. grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)); creates a fully responsive grid of cards that automatically wraps to the next line without requiring any media queries. The cards will be at least 250px wide, but will grow to fill available space evenly.
  • Overlapping Content: Unlike Flexbox or older layout methods, CSS Grid allows you to explicitly overlap elements by placing them in the same grid cells or assigning them overlapping grid-area values. You can then use z-index to control the stacking order. This opens up entirely new design possibilities for complex editorial layouts or overlapping images and text.
  • Full-Bleed Layouts: Creating a layout where the main content is constrained to a central column, but certain elements (like hero images or callout blocks) break out to span the full width of the viewport, is incredibly easy with Grid. You define a grid with three columns (e.g., 1fr minmax(auto, 800px) 1fr), place standard content in the center column, and allow full-bleed elements to span all three columns.
  • Named Grid Lines: While you can refer to grid lines by number, you can also name them for easier reference. E.g., grid-template-columns: [main-start] 1fr [content-start] 500px [content-end] 1fr [main-end];. This makes positioning items much more semantic and readable.
  • Subgrid (Level 2 Specification): CSS Grid Level 2 introduces the subgrid feature. Subgrid allows grid items that are themselves grid containers to inherit the sizing of the grid tracks from their parent grid. This solves the long-standing problem of aligning content nested within separate grid items, such as aligning card headers, bodies, and footers across a row of independently sized cards.

Choosing Between Flexbox and Grid

  • Flexbox is for one-dimensional layouts – laying things out in a single row OR a single column.
  • Grid is for two-dimensional layouts – laying things out in rows AND columns simultaneously.
  • Flexbox is content-out: You use Flexbox when you have a collection of items, and you want them to distribute themselves within a container based on their sizes and the available space. The items drive the layout.
  • Grid is layout-in: You use Grid when you have a specific layout structure in mind, and you want to place items into that predefined structure. The container drives the layout.
  • They work perfectly together: The most robust layouts use both. You might use Grid for the overall page structure (header, sidebar, main content, footer) and use Flexbox for the UI elements within those areas (e.g., aligning navigation links, centering an icon within a button, or laying out a row of actions).

topics.title: CSS Transitions & Transforms
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > CSS > Animations

CSS Transitions & Transforms: Bringing Interfaces to Life

Interactive ⏱️ 15 min read Updated: July 2026

Introduction to CSS Transitions: CSS transitions provide a way to control animation speed when changing CSS properties. Instead of having property changes take effect immediately, you can cause the changes in a property to take place over a period of time. For example, if you change the color of an element from white to black, usually the change is instantaneous. With CSS transitions enabled, changes occur at time intervals that follow an acceleration curve, all of which can be customized.

Transitions are triggered by a change in a property's value, which is most often caused by a pseudo-class like :hover, :focus, or :active, or by a class being dynamically added or removed via JavaScript.

The Four Transition Properties

  • transition-property: Specifies the name or names of the CSS properties to which transitions should be applied. Only properties listed here are animated during transitions; changes to all other properties occur instantaneously. Commonly animated properties include background-color, color, width, height, opacity, and transform. You can also use the keyword all to transition every animatable property.
  • transition-duration: Specifies the duration over which transitions should occur. You can specify a single duration that applies to all properties during the transition, or multiple values to allow each property to transition over a different period of time. Values are specified in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms).
  • transition-timing-function: Specifies a function to define how intermediate values for properties are computed. Timing functions determine how the speed of the transition varies over its duration.
    • linear: The transition has a constant speed from start to end.
    • ease: (Default) The transition starts slowly, accelerates in the middle, and slows down at the end.
    • ease-in: Starts slowly, then speeds up.
    • ease-out: Starts quickly, then slows down at the end.
    • ease-in-out: Starts and ends slowly.
    • cubic-bezier(n,n,n,n): Allows you to define your own custom acceleration curve.
  • transition-delay: Defines how long to wait between the time a property is changed and the transition actually begins.

The transition Shorthand

It is almost always easier to use the transition shorthand property rather than writing out all four properties individually. The order of values matters only for the duration and delay: the first time value parsed is assigned to transition-duration, and the second time value is assigned to transition-delay.

.button {
  background-color: #10b981;
  transform: scale(1);
  /* shorthand: property duration timing-function delay */
  transition: background-color 0.3s ease, transform 0.3s cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1);
}

.button:hover {
  background-color: #059669;
  transform: scale(1.05) translateY(-3px);
}

CSS Transforms (2D and 3D)

The transform property allows you to visually manipulate elements by rotating, scaling, skewing, or translating (moving) them in 2D or 3D space. Crucially, transforms do not affect the document flow; an element that is scaled up via transform will visually overlap other elements rather than pushing them away, making transforms incredibly performant for animations because they don't trigger browser repaints or reflows.

  • translate(x, y), translateX(x), translateY(y): Moves an element from its current position along the X and Y axes. Percentage values refer to the element's own dimensions. For example, transform: translateX(-50%) moves the element left by half of its own width.
  • scale(x, y), scaleX(x), scaleY(y): Increases or decreases the size of an element. A value of 1 represents the original size. Values between 0 and 1 shrink the element, while values greater than 1 enlarge it. Negative values will flip the element.
  • rotate(angle): Rotates an element clockwise or counter-clockwise around its origin (which can be changed using the transform-origin property). The angle can be specified in degrees (deg), radians (rad), gradians (grad), or turns (turn).
  • skew(x-angle, y-angle), skewX(angle), skewY(angle): Tilts an element along the X and/or Y axes by the given angle.

3D Transforms

CSS also supports 3D transformations, allowing you to manipulate elements along the Z-axis (depth). To create realistic 3D effects, you must apply the perspective property to a parent element, which establishes a 3D viewing space.

  • translateZ(z), translate3d(x, y, z): Moves the element along the Z-axis (closer to or further from the viewer).
  • rotateX(angle), rotateY(angle), rotateZ(angle): Rotates the element around the specific 3D axis. Rotating around the Y-axis creates a flipping effect like turning a card.
  • perspective(d): Can be applied as a transform function on the element itself, or as a property on the parent container, to give 3D-positioned elements some perspective (the illusion of depth).

topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > CSS > Animations

CSS Keyframe Animations: Advanced Motion Control

Advanced FX ⏱️ 15 min read Updated: July 2026

Introduction to CSS Animations: While CSS transitions are excellent for simple A-to-B state changes (like hovering over a button), they are limited. They require a trigger (like a hover state) and only go from a start state to an end state. When you need complex, multi-step animations that run automatically, loop indefinitely, or pause and resume, you need CSS Animations and the @keyframes rule.

An animation lets an element gradually change from one style to another. You can change as many CSS properties as you want, as many times as you want. To use CSS animation, you must first specify some keyframes for the animation. Keyframes hold what styles the element will have at certain times.

The @keyframes Rule

The @keyframes rule is where you define the stages of your animation. Inside the rule, you use percentages to specify when the style change should happen, or the keywords from (equivalent to 0%) and to (equivalent to 100%).

@keyframes Declaration Example
@keyframes pulseGlow {
  0% {
    transform: scale(1);
    box-shadow: 0 0 0 0 rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.7);
  }
  50% {
    transform: scale(1.05);
    box-shadow: 0 0 20px 10px rgba(16, 185, 129, 0.3);
  }
  100% {
    transform: scale(1);
    box-shadow: 0 0 0 0 rgba(16, 185, 129, 0);
  }
}

Animation Properties

Once your keyframes are defined, you must apply the animation to an element using the animation properties. There are several individual properties to control the behavior of the animation:

  • animation-name: Specifies the name of the @keyframes animation you want to bind to the selector.
  • animation-duration: Defines how long an animation should take to complete one cycle (in seconds or milliseconds). If this is not specified, the animation will not play, because the default value is 0.
  • animation-timing-function: Specifies the speed curve of the animation, exactly like transition-timing-function. It accepts values like ease, linear, ease-in-out, or cubic-bezier(). It also accepts steps(n), which allows you to create blocky, frame-by-frame animations instead of smooth interpolations.
  • animation-delay: Specifies a delay before the animation will start. Negative values are allowed; if you set a negative delay (e.g., -2s), the animation will start immediately, but as if it had already been playing for 2 seconds.
  • animation-iteration-count: Specifies the number of times an animation should be played. It accepts an integer, or the keyword infinite to make the animation loop forever.
  • animation-direction: Specifies whether an animation should be played forwards, backwards, or in alternate cycles.
    • normal: (Default) Plays forwards from 0% to 100%.
    • reverse: Plays backwards from 100% to 0%.
    • alternate: Plays forwards first, then backwards.
    • alternate-reverse: Plays backwards first, then forwards.
  • animation-fill-mode: Specifies a style for the element when the animation is not playing (before it starts, after it ends, or both). By default, CSS animations do not affect the element before the first keyframe is played or after the last keyframe is played.
    • forwards: The element will retain the style values that is set by the last keyframe (depends on animation-direction and animation-iteration-count).
    • backwards: The element will get the style values that is set by the first keyframe (depends on animation-direction), and retain this during the animation-delay period.
    • both: The animation will follow the rules for both forwards and backwards, extending the animation properties in both directions.
  • animation-play-state: Specifies whether the animation is running or paused. This is extremely useful for pausing an animation when the user hovers over an element, using the paused keyword.

The animation Shorthand

Like transitions, animations have a shorthand property to keep your CSS clean and concise. The order of values is generally: name duration timing-function delay iteration-count direction fill-mode play-state.

.glowing-badge {
  /* Using the shorthand property */
  animation: pulseGlow 2s ease-in-out 0s infinite normal none running;
  /* Simplified common usage */
  animation: pulseGlow 2s infinite ease-in-out;
}

Performance Considerations for Animations

When creating animations, performance is crucial for ensuring a smooth, 60-frames-per-second (FPS) experience. The browser's rendering engine goes through several steps: Layout, Paint, and Composite. Animating properties that trigger Layout (like width, height, margin, top, left) or Paint (like color, background, box-shadow) is computationally expensive and can cause stuttering (jank).

For the best performance, you should restrict your animations to properties that only trigger the Composite step. Modern browsers can hand off these properties directly to the GPU for hardware-accelerated rendering. The most performant properties to animate are transform (translate, scale, rotate, skew) and opacity. By sticking to these properties, you guarantee buttery-smooth animations across all devices, from high-end desktops to low-powered mobile phones.

Advanced Pseudo-Elements (::before, ::after) & Pseudo-Classes

Advanced ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

Pseudo-classes target elements in specific states (e.g. :nth-child(), :not(), :focus-within), while Pseudo-elements style specific sub-parts or inject decorative elements into the DOM without extra HTML tags.

/* Injecting decorative gradient line using ::after */
.section-title {
  position: relative;
  display: inline-block;
  margin-bottom: 2rem;
}

.section-title::after {
  content: '';
  position: absolute;
  bottom: -8px;
  left: 0;
  width: 60%;
  height: 3px;
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, #10b981, transparent);
  border-radius: 2px;
}

/* Target structural nth-child */
.list-item:nth-child(odd) {
  background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.03);
}

/* Target elements NOT matching selector */
.btn:not(.btn-disabled):hover {
  cursor: pointer;
}

Media Queries (@media) & Mobile-First Responsive Design

Responsive ⏱️ 9 min read Updated: July 2026

Media queries are a key feature of CSS3 that allow content rendering to adapt to conditions such as screen resolution, viewport width, device orientation, and color scheme preferences.

📱 Common Breakpoint Standard

  • 320px - 480px: Mobile devices
  • 481px - 768px: iPads & Tablets
  • 769px - 1024px: Laptops & Small Screens
  • 1025px - 1200px+: Desktops & Large Displays
/* Mobile-First Approach: Base styles for mobile */
.sidebar {
  display: none; /* Hidden on narrow screens */
}

/* Tablet & Desktop breakpoint override */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .sidebar {
    display: block;
    width: 280px;
  }
  
  .main-content {
    margin-left: 280px;
  }
}

/* Dark / Light Preference detection */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  body {
    background-color: #0f172a;
    color: #f8fafc;
  }
}

topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > CSS > Advanced

Z-Index Property & Stacking Context Hierarchy

Depth Engine ⏱️ 7 min read Updated: July 2026

The z-index property specifies the stack order of an element. An element with greater stack order is always in front of an element with a lower stack order.

⚠️ Important Rule

z-index ONLY works on positioned elements (e.g. position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky) and flex/grid child items!

.modal-backdrop {
  position: fixed;
  top: 0;
  left: 0;
  width: 100vw;
  height: 100vh;
  background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.75);
  z-index: 999; /* Under dialog, above page */
}

.modal-dialog {
  position: fixed;
  top: 50%;
  left: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
  z-index: 1000; /* Highest priority layer */
}

Bootstrap Framework: Grid System & Utility Classes

Framework ⏱️ 10 min read Updated: July 2026

Bootstrap is the world's most popular front-end open-source toolkit. It features a 12-column responsive flexbox grid system, extensive prebuilt components, and powerful utility classes.

12-Column Responsive Grid System

<div class="container">
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-8">
      <h2>Main Content (8 cols on desktop, 12 on mobile)</h2>
    </div>
    <div class="col-12 col-md-4">
      <aside>Sidebar (4 cols on desktop)</aside>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Bootstrap vs Pure Custom CSS Comparison

Feature Bootstrap Framework Pure Custom CSS
Development Speed ⚡ Rapid prototyping using ready components 🛠️ Custom built from ground up
File Size & Control Includes framework overhead unless purged Zero overhead, 100% granular design control
Consistency Standardized design tokens across teams Requires custom design system rules

quiz.question: When 'box-sizing: border-box' is applied to an element with width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 5px solid black, what is the computed total rendered width of the element on screen?
quiz.explanation: With 'box-sizing: border-box', the specified width encompasses padding and borders. The content width shrinks to 300 - (2 * 20) - (2 * 5) = 250px, but the total rendered box width remains exactly 300px.

quiz.question: Under the default 'box-sizing: content-box', what would be the total rendered width for an element with width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 5px?
quiz.explanation: In content-box, width applies solely to the inner content area. Total width = width (300px) + left/right padding (40px) + left/right border (10px) = 350px.

quiz.question: Which of the following CSS selectors has the highest specificity weight?
quiz.explanation: 'div#nav a.active' has 1 ID, 1 class, and 2 elements: (0, 1, 1, 2). '#main-navigation' has (0, 1, 0, 0). (0, 1, 1, 2) is higher than (0, 1, 0, 0).

quiz.question: What is the primary difference between 'display: none' and 'visibility: hidden'?
options: 'display: none' removes the element from normal layout flow and it occupies zero space; 'visibility: hidden' makes it invisible while preserving its physical layout footprint
'visibility: hidden' removes the element from the DOM tree
quiz.explanation: 'display: none' prevents element box generation in layout. 'visibility: hidden' renders an invisible box, maintaining its exact width, height, and layout position.

quiz.question: In CSS Flexbox, which property aligns flex items along the primary axis (main axis)?
quiz.explanation: 'justify-content' aligns flex items along the main axis (horizontal by default in row direction). 'align-items' controls alignment along the cross axis.

quiz.question: In Flexbox, what does the shorthand declaration 'flex: 1' expand to?
quiz.explanation: The unitless shorthand 'flex: 1' sets flex-grow to 1, flex-shrink to 1, and flex-basis to 0% (or 0 in standard W3C flexbox specs).

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'align-items' and 'align-content' in a Flexbox container?
options: 'align-items' aligns items within a single flex line; 'align-content' aligns the flex lines themselves along the cross axis when there is extra space and flex-wrap is enabled
quiz.explanation: 'align-content' only has an effect in multi-line flex containers (flex-wrap: wrap) with free space along the cross axis. It aligns the lines relative to each other.

quiz.question: How does the 'position: absolute' property position an element?
options: Relative to the root HTML element only
Relative to the closest ancestor element that has a position property other than 'static' (containing block)
Relative to its immediate parent regardless of position property
Relative to the browser window always
quiz.explanation: An absolute element is removed from normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (an ancestor with position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky). If none exists, it positions relative to the initial containing block.

quiz.question: What makes 'position: sticky' unique compared to 'relative' and 'fixed'?
options: It locks the element into the center of the viewport
It acts as 'position: relative' until its container scrolls past a threshold (e.g. top: 0), where it behaves as 'position: fixed' within its parent boundaries
It makes elements stick to the mouse cursor
quiz.explanation: 'position: sticky' is a hybrid: the element scrolls normally until it reaches a specified offset, at which point it sticks in place until its parent container scrolls out of view.

quiz.question: What is the difference between the CSS units 'em' and 'rem'?
options: 'em' is relative to the root (<html>) font size; 'rem' is relative to the immediate parent's font size
'em' is relative to the current or immediate parent's font size; 'rem' (Root EM) is relative strictly to the root (<html>) element's font size
'em' is measured in physical inches; 'rem' is measured in screen dots
quiz.explanation: 'em' is relative to the font-size of its direct element or parent (compounding when nested). 'rem' references the root <html> font-size (usually 16px by default), avoiding cascading compounding.

quiz.question: What causes vertical margin collapsing in standard CSS flow?
options: Negative margins cancel each other out
Adjacent top and bottom margins of block elements in the normal flow combine into a single margin equal to the maximum of the two margins
Margins collapse when padding is applied
Only flexbox children experience margin collapsing
quiz.explanation: Margin collapsing occurs when vertical margins of adjoining block-level boxes in normal flow merge into a single margin (the larger of the two). Margins never collapse on flex, grid, or absolute items.

quiz.question: How do you define a responsive CSS Grid column layout where columns are at least 250px wide and expand equally to fill the viewport?
quiz.explanation: 'repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))' automatically creates as many columns as fit into the container with a minimum of 250px, stretching equally to fill leftover space.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'auto-fill' and 'auto-fit' in CSS Grid repeat() syntax?
options: 'auto-fill' creates empty ghost tracks if space permits; 'auto-fit' collapses empty tracks to 0px, expanding populated columns to take up all remaining width
'auto-fit' only works with fixed pixel widths
quiz.explanation: 'auto-fill' maintains the calculated number of tracks even if empty. 'auto-fit' collapses empty tracks to 0, allowing actual items to stretch and fill all available container space.

quiz.question: Which property controls the stacking order of overlapping positioned elements on the screen?
quiz.explanation: The 'z-index' property specifies the z-axis stack order of positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) or direct flex/grid children.

quiz.question: Which of the following conditions creates a new Stacking Context in CSS?
options: Setting 'opacity' to a value less than 1
Setting 'transform' to any value other than 'none'
Setting 'filter' to any value other than 'none'
quiz.explanation: A new stacking context is generated by opacity < 1, transform/filter/perspective != none, position: fixed/sticky, will-change, or container isolation, constraining child z-indexes within that local context.

quiz.question: What does the ':nth-child(2n)' pseudo-class select?
quiz.explanation: ':nth-child(2n)' matches all even child elements (formula: 2*0=0, 2*1=2, 2*2=4...), identical to ':nth-child(even)'.

quiz.question: What is the difference between ':nth-child()' and ':nth-of-type()'?
options: ':nth-child(n)' counts elements among ALL sibling tags regardless of type; ':nth-of-type(n)' counts elements strictly among siblings sharing the same tag name
quiz.explanation:
In 'p:nth-child(2)', the element must be the 2nd child of its parent AND a

. In 'p:nth-of-type(2)', it selects the 2nd

element among siblings, ignoring any non-

tags.

quiz.question: What is mandatory on the '::before' and '::after' pseudo-elements for them to render on the page?
quiz.explanation: Pseudo-elements ::before and ::after will not generate a box or render at all unless the 'content' property is declared (even if empty: content: '').

quiz.question: How do you declare and access a CSS Custom Property (CSS Variable)?
quiz.explanation: Native CSS variables are declared with two leading hyphens (e.g. --main-color: #3b82f6) and referenced via the var(--main-color, fallback) function.

quiz.question: What does the 'clamp()' CSS function do?
options: Animates the font size back and forth
Clamps a value between an absolute minimum (1rem), a preferred dynamic value (2.5vw), and an absolute maximum (2rem)
Rounds the font size to the nearest whole integer
quiz.explanation: clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX) clamps the value between an allowed minimum and maximum, ideal for fluid responsive typography without media queries.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the modern CSS ':has()' relational pseudo-class selector?
options: Selects the image inside the article

Acts as a 'parent selector', styling the
if it contains at least one descendant element
Checks if the browser has cached the article
Applies styles only when JavaScript is loaded
quiz.explanation:
':has()' is CSS's long-awaited parent/relational selector. 'article:has(img)' targets the
element itself if it contains an .

quiz.question: What is the difference between ':is()' and ':where()' in modern CSS?
options: ':is()' has zero specificity; ':where()' takes the highest specificity
':is()' takes the specificity of its most specific selector argument; ':where()' always has ZERO specificity (0, 0, 0, 0)
quiz.explanation: Both reduce selector duplication, but ':where()' always has 0 specificity, making it ideal for CSS reset and default utility rules that are easy to override.

quiz.question: What does 'animation-fill-mode: forwards' specify?
options: The animation plays forward and then in reverse
The target element retains the computed style values from the last keyframe after the animation finishes
The animation applies styles before starting
quiz.explanation: 'animation-fill-mode: forwards' causes the element to retain the styling defined in the final keyframe (100% or 'to') after the animation ends.

quiz.question: Which CSS property enables GPU hardware acceleration for smooth 60fps animations?
quiz.explanation: Applying 3D transforms (translate3d/translateZ) or 'will-change: transform' promotes the element to its own GPU compositor layer, bypassing expensive main-thread CPU repaints.

quiz.question: What is the CSS 'gap' property used for?
options: Sets the margin around the body element
Defines the gutter spacing between rows and columns in Flexbox and CSS Grid containers without adding outer margins
quiz.explanation: 'gap' (and row-gap/column-gap) sets gutters between children in CSS Grid and modern Flexbox without needing negative margins on wrappers.

quiz.question: What does the 'contain: strict' or 'contain: content' property do in CSS?
options: Locks the aspect ratio of images
Tells the browser engine that the element's subtree is completely isolated from the rest of the DOM, enabling massive layout/paint performance optimizations
quiz.explanation: CSS Containment (contain: layout paint size) isolates an element's rendering subtree, so the browser doesn't have to recompute the entire page layout on internal DOM mutations.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'opacity: 0' and 'pointer-events: none'?
options: 'opacity: 0' makes the element visually transparent but it still receives mouse clicks and blocks underlying elements; 'pointer-events: none' allows clicks to pass straight through the element to layers underneath
'opacity: 0' removes the element from the DOM
quiz.explanation: 'opacity: 0' elements still intercept mouse events and block clicks to layers below. 'pointer-events: none' disables click and hover interception, letting events pass through.

quiz.question: What does the 'backdrop-filter: blur(10px)' property do?
options: Blurs the foreground text of the element
Applies a graphical blur effect to the area BEHIND the element (essential for frosted-glass glassmorphism design)
quiz.explanation: Unlike 'filter: blur()', which blurs the element itself, 'backdrop-filter: blur()' filters the pixels rendered directly behind a semi-transparent element, creating frosted glass.

quiz.question: Which CSS property is used to truncate overflow text with an ellipsis (...)?
options: text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden;
quiz.explanation: Single-line text truncation requires the triumvirate: 'overflow: hidden', 'white-space: nowrap', and 'text-overflow: ellipsis'.

quiz.question: What does the 'aspect-ratio' property achieve in modern CSS?
options: Sets the focal length of responsive cameras
Enforces a defined width-to-height ratio on an element without requiring padding-top layout hacks
quiz.explanation: The 'aspect-ratio: 16 / 9' property allows browsers to automatically calculate the element's height based on its width, reserving layout space and preventing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

All

quiz.explanation: The '+' combinator selects the element immediately preceded by the former element with the same parent. (The general sibling combinator '~' selects all subsequent siblings).

All

elements that follow

sharing the same parent, even if separated by other tags
quiz.explanation: The general sibling combinator '~' matches all sibling elements that occur anywhere after the reference element under the same parent.

quiz.question: What does 'transform-origin' control?
options: The location of the original file
The point of origin around which transforms (rotation, scaling, skewing) are calculated (default is 50% 50% 0)
quiz.explanation: 'transform-origin' sets the pivot point for geometric transformations. By default, it is centered at '50% 50%' (the center of the element's bounding box).

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'currentColor' and standard color keywords in CSS?
options: 'currentColor' is a CSS keyword that takes the computed value of the element's current 'color' property, enabling dynamic SVG icon fills and borders
quiz.explanation: 'currentColor' dynamically inherits the value of the CSS 'color' property, allowing SVG fills, borders, and shadows to automatically adapt to text color changes.

quiz.question: What does the 'overscroll-behavior: contain' property prevent?
options: Prevents scroll chaining and browser bounce/pull-to-refresh when reaching scroll boundaries inside a modal or drawer
quiz.explanation: 'overscroll-behavior: contain' prevents scrolling from propagating to parent containers (scroll chaining) when the inner container reaches its boundary.

quiz.question: Which pseudo-class applies styles when an element is focused specifically via keyboard navigation (e.g. Tab key) rather than a mouse click?
quiz.explanation: ':focus-visible' only activates when the user interacts using a non-pointing device (like a keyboard), keeping visual focus rings for accessibility while removing them for mouse clicks.

quiz.question: What does the ':focus-within' pseudo-class match?
options: The form itself if it has autofocus
The container element if the element itself OR ANY of its descendants has focus
The first input of the form
quiz.explanation: ':focus-within' targets a parent element if any of its children currently possess focus (e.g., highlighting an entire form card when typing inside an input).

quiz.question: How does the 'calc()' CSS function handle operator spacing?
options: Spaces are mandatory around addition (+) and subtraction (-) operators to differentiate them from negative numbers
Spaces are only allowed around division
quiz.explanation: In calc(), the '+' and '-' operators MUST have whitespace on both sides (e.g. '100% - 20px', not '100%-20px') because a minus without spaces is parsed as a negative sign.

quiz.question: What is the CSS cascade hierarchy order from lowest to highest priority?
options: User styles -> Browser default (User Agent) -> Author styles
Browser default (User Agent) -> User normal styles -> Author normal styles -> Author !important -> User !important
quiz.explanation: The CSS Cascade evaluates origins: Browser defaults (User Agent) are lowest, followed by User normal styles, Author normal styles, Author !important, and finally User !important as highest.

quiz.question: What does '@layer' (Cascade Layers) allow developers to do in modern CSS?
options: Explicitly controls the cascade precedence and specificity order between different stylesheets (e.g. ensuring component styles always override third-party framework styles)
quiz.explanation: Cascade Layers (@layer) give developers explicit control over the cascade order regardless of selector specificity, resolving third-party CSS specificity wars.

quiz.question: What does the 'line-height: 1.5' unitless number mean?
options: Multiplies the element's computed font-size by 1.5 to determine line box height without inheriting fixed pixel values to children
quiz.explanation: A unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) scales proportionally with the font-size of each descendant element, preventing overlapping text that happens with inherited fixed units.

quiz.question: What does the 'isolation: isolate' property accomplish?
options: Isolates the element in an iframe
Creates a new Stacking Context without needing to set opacity, transform, or z-index
Disconnects the element from the DOM
quiz.explanation: 'isolation: isolate' creates a new stacking context on the element cleanly, preventing child z-indexes and mix-blend-modes from bleeding into outer siblings.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'filter: drop-shadow()' and 'box-shadow'?
options: 'box-shadow' draws a rectangular shadow conforming to the element's box model; 'filter: drop-shadow()' conforms to the actual transparent contours and alpha channel of PNG/SVG shapes
quiz.explanation: 'box-shadow' creates a shadow around the rectangular box. 'filter: drop-shadow()' traces the transparent alpha channel of PNG images and SVGs, casting shadows around the actual artwork.

quiz.question: What does the 'ch' unit represent in CSS?
options: The advance width of the character '0' (zero) in the element's current font (ideal for limiting line lengths in reading typography)
quiz.explanation: The 'ch' unit equals the width of the character '0' in the current font. Setting 'max-width: 65ch' is the gold standard for comfortable reading typography (45-75 chars/line).

quiz.question: What does the 'font-display: swap' descriptor do in an '@font-face' rule?
options: Instructs the browser to render text immediately using a fallback system font, swapping to the custom web font as soon as it downloads (eliminating Flash of Invisible Text - FOIT)
Disables web fonts on slow connections
quiz.explanation: 'font-display: swap' eliminates FOIT (Flash of Invisible Text) by using a fallback font during download, then instantly swapping to the custom font once loaded.

quiz.question: What does 'scrollbar-gutter: stable' do in modern CSS?
options: Reserves space for the scrollbar beforehand, preventing jarring layout shifts when scrollable content appears and disappears
quiz.explanation: 'scrollbar-gutter: stable' reserves layout space for the scrollbar gutter, preventing content jumping horizontally when scrollbars toggle on dynamic page heights.

options: Form inputs that contain no value
Elements that have no child nodes at all (including text nodes and whitespace)
quiz.explanation: ':empty' matches elements that have zero child elements and zero text nodes (even whitespace counts as a child text node unless using modern ':blank').

quiz.question: What does the 'pointer-events: none' property do when applied to an element?
options: Changes the cursor to a pointer
Prevents the element from receiving mouse/touch events (clicks, hovers), allowing events to pass through to underlying elements
quiz.explanation: 'pointer-events: none' prevents mouse, touch, and click events from targeting the element. Events pass directly through to whatever elements are positioned beneath.

CSS Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) - 50 Practice Questions

Assessment ⏱️ 60 min 50 Questions

Test and master your CSS and CSS3 knowledge with this comprehensive set of 50 Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) formatted in the classic GeeksforGeeks tutorial assessment style. Covering box model, specificity, flexbox, CSS grid, positioning, transitions, animations, modern selectors (:has, :is, :where), custom properties, and container queries.

📝 Assessment Instructions

  • Each question has four potential choices: (A), (B), (C), and (D).
  • Review the problem statement and code snippet carefully before picking your answer.
  • Click on "💡 View Answer & Explanation" to reveal the correct option along with an in-depth technical explanation.

Question 1: When 'box-sizing: border-box' is applied to an element with width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 5px solid black, what is the computed total rendered width of the element on screen?

2 Points 
div {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: 300px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid black;
}
A) 350px
B) 300px ✓ Correct
C) 250px
D) 325px
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 300px

Explanation: With 'box-sizing: border-box', the specified width encompasses padding and borders. The content width shrinks to 300 - (2 * 20) - (2 * 5) = 250px, but the total rendered box width remains exactly 300px.

Question 2: Under the default 'box-sizing: content-box', what would be the total rendered width for an element with width: 300px, padding: 20px, and border: 5px?

2 Points
A) 300px
B) 325px
C) 350px ✓ Correct
D) 275px
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (C) 350px

Explanation: In content-box, width applies solely to the inner content area. Total width = width (300px) + left/right padding (40px) + left/right border (10px) = 350px.

Question 3: Which of the following CSS selectors has the highest specificity weight?

2 Points
A) div.container ul.nav li a:hover
B) #main-navigation
C) body > header.site-header nav
D) div#nav a.active ✓ Correct
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (D) div#nav a.active

Explanation: 'div#nav a.active' has 1 ID, 1 class, and 2 elements: (0, 1, 1, 2). '#main-navigation' has (0, 1, 0, 0). (0, 1, 1, 2) is higher than (0, 1, 0, 0).

Question 4: What is the primary difference between 'display: none' and 'visibility: hidden'?

2 Points
A) No functional difference
B) 'display: none' removes the element from normal layout flow and it occupies zero space; 'visibility: hidden' makes it invisible while preserving its physical layout footprint ✓ Correct
C) 'visibility: hidden' removes the element from the DOM tree
D) 'display: none' triggers screen reader announcements
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'display: none' removes the element from normal layout flow and it occupies zero space; 'visibility: hidden' makes it invisible while preserving its physical layout footprint

Explanation: 'display: none' prevents element box generation in layout. 'visibility: hidden' renders an invisible box, maintaining its exact width, height, and layout position.

Question 5: In CSS Flexbox, which property aligns flex items along the primary axis (main axis)?

2 Points
A) align-items
B) justify-content ✓ Correct
C) align-content
D) flex-direction
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) justify-content

Explanation: 'justify-content' aligns flex items along the main axis (horizontal by default in row direction). 'align-items' controls alignment along the cross axis.

Question 6: In Flexbox, what does the shorthand declaration 'flex: 1' expand to?

2 Points
A) flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%; ✓ Correct
B) flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 0; flex-basis: auto;
C) flex-grow: 0; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 100%;
D) flex-direction: row; flex-wrap: nowrap;
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (A) flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0%;

Explanation: The unitless shorthand 'flex: 1' sets flex-grow to 1, flex-shrink to 1, and flex-basis to 0% (or 0 in standard W3C flexbox specs).

Question 7: What is the difference between 'align-items' and 'align-content' in a Flexbox container?

2 Points
A) There is no difference
B) 'align-items' aligns items within a single flex line; 'align-content' aligns the flex lines themselves along the cross axis when there is extra space and flex-wrap is enabled ✓ Correct
C) 'align-content' aligns text only
D) 'align-items' only works in CSS Grid
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'align-items' aligns items within a single flex line; 'align-content' aligns the flex lines themselves along the cross axis when there is extra space and flex-wrap is enabled

Explanation: 'align-content' only has an effect in multi-line flex containers (flex-wrap: wrap) with free space along the cross axis. It aligns the lines relative to each other.

Question 8: How does the 'position: absolute' property position an element?

2 Points
A) Relative to the root HTML element only
B) Relative to the closest ancestor element that has a position property other than 'static' (containing block) ✓ Correct
C) Relative to its immediate parent regardless of position property
D) Relative to the browser window always
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Relative to the closest ancestor element that has a position property other than 'static' (containing block)

Explanation: An absolute element is removed from normal flow and positioned relative to its nearest positioned ancestor (an ancestor with position: relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky). If none exists, it positions relative to the initial containing block.

Question 9: What makes 'position: sticky' unique compared to 'relative' and 'fixed'?

2 Points
A) It locks the element into the center of the viewport
B) It acts as 'position: relative' until its container scrolls past a threshold (e.g. top: 0), where it behaves as 'position: fixed' within its parent boundaries ✓ Correct
C) It makes elements stick to the mouse cursor
D) It permanently disables scrolling
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) It acts as 'position: relative' until its container scrolls past a threshold (e.g. top: 0), where it behaves as 'position: fixed' within its parent boundaries

Explanation: 'position: sticky' is a hybrid: the element scrolls normally until it reaches a specified offset, at which point it sticks in place until its parent container scrolls out of view.

Question 10: What is the difference between the CSS units 'em' and 'rem'?

2 Points
A) 'em' is relative to the root () font size; 'rem' is relative to the immediate parent's font size
B) 'em' is relative to the current or immediate parent's font size; 'rem' (Root EM) is relative strictly to the root () element's font size ✓ Correct
C) 'em' is measured in physical inches; 'rem' is measured in screen dots
D) 'rem' is deprecated in CSS3
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'em' is relative to the current or immediate parent's font size; 'rem' (Root EM) is relative strictly to the root () element's font size

Explanation: 'em' is relative to the font-size of its direct element or parent (compounding when nested). 'rem' references the root font-size (usually 16px by default), avoiding cascading compounding.

Question 11: What causes vertical margin collapsing in standard CSS flow?

2 Points
A) Negative margins cancel each other out
B) Adjacent top and bottom margins of block elements in the normal flow combine into a single margin equal to the maximum of the two margins ✓ Correct
C) Margins collapse when padding is applied
D) Only flexbox children experience margin collapsing
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Adjacent top and bottom margins of block elements in the normal flow combine into a single margin equal to the maximum of the two margins

Explanation: Margin collapsing occurs when vertical margins of adjoining block-level boxes in normal flow merge into a single margin (the larger of the two). Margins never collapse on flex, grid, or absolute items.

Question 12: How do you define a responsive CSS Grid column layout where columns are at least 250px wide and expand equally to fill the viewport?

2 Points
A) grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)); ✓ Correct
B) grid-template-columns: auto 250px 1fr;
C) grid-columns: flex(250px, 100%);
D) grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 250px);
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (A) grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));

Explanation: 'repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))' automatically creates as many columns as fit into the container with a minimum of 250px, stretching equally to fill leftover space.

Question 13: What is the difference between 'auto-fill' and 'auto-fit' in CSS Grid repeat() syntax?

2 Points
A) No difference
B) 'auto-fill' creates empty ghost tracks if space permits; 'auto-fit' collapses empty tracks to 0px, expanding populated columns to take up all remaining width ✓ Correct
C) 'auto-fit' only works with fixed pixel widths
D) 'auto-fill' requires media queries
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'auto-fill' creates empty ghost tracks if space permits; 'auto-fit' collapses empty tracks to 0px, expanding populated columns to take up all remaining width

Explanation: 'auto-fill' maintains the calculated number of tracks even if empty. 'auto-fit' collapses empty tracks to 0, allowing actual items to stretch and fill all available container space.

Question 14: Which property controls the stacking order of overlapping positioned elements on the screen?

2 Points
A) layer-index
B) z-index ✓ Correct
C) elevation
D) depth
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) z-index

Explanation: The 'z-index' property specifies the z-axis stack order of positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) or direct flex/grid children.

Question 15: Which of the following conditions creates a new Stacking Context in CSS?

2 Points
A) Setting 'opacity' to a value less than 1
B) Setting 'transform' to any value other than 'none'
C) Setting 'filter' to any value other than 'none'
D) All of the above ✓ Correct
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (D) All of the above

Explanation: A new stacking context is generated by opacity < 1, transform/filter/perspective != none, position: fixed/sticky, will-change, or container isolation, constraining child z-indexes within that local context.

Question 16: What does the ':nth-child(2n)' pseudo-class select?

2 Points
A) The second child only
B) All even-numbered child elements (2nd, 4th, 6th, etc.) ✓ Correct
C) All odd-numbered child elements (1st, 3rd, 5th, etc.)
D) Every 20th element
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) All even-numbered child elements (2nd, 4th, 6th, etc.)

Explanation: ':nth-child(2n)' matches all even child elements (formula: 2*0=0, 2*1=2, 2*2=4...), identical to ':nth-child(even)'.

Question 17: What is the difference between ':nth-child()' and ':nth-of-type()'?

2 Points
A) There is no difference
B) ':nth-child(n)' counts elements among ALL sibling tags regardless of type; ':nth-of-type(n)' counts elements strictly among siblings sharing the same tag name ✓ Correct
C) ':nth-of-type()' only selects class names
D) ':nth-child()' is deprecated in CSS3
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) ':nth-child(n)' counts elements among ALL sibling tags regardless of type; ':nth-of-type(n)' counts elements strictly among siblings sharing the same tag name

Explanation: In 'p:nth-child(2)', the element must be the 2nd child of its parent AND a

element among siblings, ignoring any non-

tags.

Question 18: What is mandatory on the '::before' and '::after' pseudo-elements for them to render on the page?

2 Points
A) display: block
B) content: '' (content property must be defined) ✓ Correct
C) position: absolute
D) width: 100%
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) content: '' (content property must be defined)

Explanation: Pseudo-elements ::before and ::after will not generate a box or render at all unless the 'content' property is declared (even if empty: content: '').

Question 19: How do you declare and access a CSS Custom Property (CSS Variable)?

2 Points
A) Declare: $color: red; Access: $color;
B) Declare: --main-color: #3b82f6; Access: var(--main-color); ✓ Correct
C) Declare: @main-color: #3b82f6; Access: @main-color;
D) Declare: const(color, red); Access: get(color);
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Declare: --main-color: #3b82f6; Access: var(--main-color);

Explanation: Native CSS variables are declared with two leading hyphens (e.g. --main-color: #3b82f6) and referenced via the var(--main-color, fallback) function.

Question 20: What does the 'clamp()' CSS function do?

2 Points 
font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem);
A) Animates the font size back and forth
B) Clamps a value between an absolute minimum (1rem), a preferred dynamic value (2.5vw), and an absolute maximum (2rem) ✓ Correct
C) Rounds the font size to the nearest whole integer
D) Converts pixels to rems
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Clamps a value between an absolute minimum (1rem), a preferred dynamic value (2.5vw), and an absolute maximum (2rem)

Explanation: clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX) clamps the value between an allowed minimum and maximum, ideal for fluid responsive typography without media queries.

Question 21: What is the purpose of the modern CSS ':has()' relational pseudo-class selector?

B) Acts as a 'parent selector', styling the

D) Applies styles only when JavaScript is loaded
💡 View Answer & Explanation
